children.text: Same journey for me, although I still use skills. Claude Code is fine; the remote-control feature is why I stick with it now. Generally anything in the cloud doesn't have a proper GPU that supports WebGPU, and as nice as SwiftShader is often you want to actually run things on a real machine. remote-control is by far the easiest way to do that from my phone.

It used to be more interesting and elaborate, switching between different models. I used to use Cursor, then Codex, but since Opus 5.5 came out, I just use the Claude IDE. I got rid of all my skills and just set it to medium. Then I vaguely talk to it about very high-end things that I want, and it comes back with magic. Rinse and repeat.

I'd say the biggest trick is just to tell it what complete looks like. Be very specific about what you want it to come back with once it's done. That gives it a good idea what the goal is. It'll automatically create subagents and all that stuff. Although if you have money to burn and you're doing something large, you can tell it to just go wide or boil the ocean.

Also, make sure you're working on at least five different things. Otherwise, you're sitting around for one agent.

children.author: peepee1982
children.text:
It has no weak points in my experience (compared to other harnesses). It is so good that I just can't use anything else anymore without feeling frustrated.

Theo of T3 Code has made a recent video about its features.

A few examples of why I like it:

- Not having to use multiple agents (you can switch them mid-conversation with automatic handoff if you want)

- The way it handles environments (I can start a new session on any environment (machine) with two clicks (new thread -> pick project on any environment)

- I can ask for visual responses (uses a T3 Code tool and renders a html page inside chat with cards, charts, etc. that follow the currently selected color theme (even if you change the theme after the response has been generated)

- MCP tools like browser, webfetch, etc. so I don't have to set them up for every agent

- Thread handling: Snooze, Settle, Archive, Delete. It's the only tool where I don't get overwhelmed when working on multiple Threads/Projects at the same time (I am diagnosed with ADHD).

- Provider usage overview for all registered providers, showing pacing as well

- Great citation: when you make a selection in chat, a pill appears and you can create quotation elements that get added to that, can easily be edited or removed (the original reason why I even tried T3 Code in the first place, because it makes responding to long responses incredibly joyful instead of disorienting). I like it so much that I added the same mechanism to my own personal assistant/agent that I host on my VPS.

- Great diffing view where you can pick worktree diffs, or any diff from a specific turn in the current thread

- Has it's own subagent orchestration that's very pleasant to use

- Many more little things that remove a lot of friction and just feel right for me.

It's just baffling to me how it is better in every regard than every other harness that I've ever tried (Claude Desktop, Github Copilot App, OpenCode Desktop, all the CLIs, Integrated Agents in VSCode and Zed, etc.)

I will still start up a pi on the cli if I just have a quick question because T3 Code needs a bit to start up and connect to all providers/environments. This is my only point of friction: It's a bit heavy on resources (because it does a lot, not because it's slow. I just happen to use it on very old hardware and on one device that is very slowed down due to heavy-handed security scanning). But other than that, I can't imagine using anything else right now.

I don't know if I've ever been this exciting about a piece of software. I was very sceptical at first, but quickly fell in love with it.
Where do you find that T3 Code is strongest and where it is weakest?

I use T3 Code as my front-end for all my coding agents on all my personal computers and my VPS.

For the actual agents I use Claude Code for my Claude subscription, Codex for my OpenAI subscription (I usually only keep one of those at a time), and pi for my OpenCode Go subscription.

I mostly use Sonnet 5.5 medium and Sol 6.1 medium for everything. But lately I have been using DeepSeek 4.1 Flash a lot and find it very capable.

At work I use T3 Code as well, but it isn't connected to my personal machines or subscriptions and use Github Copilot in T3 Code via ACP. Model choice is similar, but for more involved tasks for architecture analysis or design, big features that touch a lot of interconnected subsystems, etc. I'll turn up reasoning effort to high or use Opus 5.5 on medium or high. But when actually implementing, I try to break up my tasks into smaller pieces and the models usually do well even without reasoning turned up.

Most of my work goes into rewriting prose in reports, commit messages, PR summaries, etc. because all models still struggle with that. (Claude models less than GPT ones in my experience, but still ...)

First off, I cannot pretend I have this solved. But I can share one thing that has worked for me, along with codex maintaining it's own local memory (turn it on).

I notice that single-threaded agents get stuck with things sometimes like writing some tool they need inefficiently so that it takes 3 hours when it could be 3 minutes (meaning that a task ends up taking days instead of hours, unless I intervene and tell it to make a fast tool instead) but subagents just compound this as they burn through tokens without realising the problem.

If you use claude code on ultracode it already spawns subagents by default now, i think agent orchestrator has the only benefit of ofloading some tokens and making the subagents to not get distracted by the bigger picture but i cant see any use case of the broader orchestration on a project that is already solid and you just push features and debug, a single session give you more ownership of what is build

source.text:
I'm curious how people on HN are using AI day to day, and came up with a list of questions I thought could be interesting to know. No need to answer every question of course, just wanted to get a gut feel how people are using AI.

1) What AI subscriptions are you personally paying for? (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, etc)

- Which tiers?

- Have you purchased multiple subscriptions from the same provider (eg two Claude accounts)?

2) Are you using models outside (or instead) of those subscriptions? For example, pay-as-you-go APIs, OpenRouter, or locally hosted models.

- Which models and providers?

3) What coding harnesses and interfaces are you using? Are you sticking with the default CLIs or IDE integrations, or using alternatives like OpenCode, Pi, Aider, Muse Code, or custom-built harnesses?

- What made you switch harnesses (if you switched)?

4) Are you using any agent orchestration or swarm tools?

- For example, Munder Difflin, Gas Town, Ruflo, or something custom.

5) Are you using broader agent platforms like OpenClaw / Hermes Agent / Grok bot / Dots / Muse?

- If you are using them, what are your main use cases?

-----

I know my workflow has differed significantly from a year ago, and so it would be interesting to capture a snapshot today of what people are using and why.

comments.author: peepee1982
comments.text: It has no weak points in my experience (compared to other harnesses). It is so good that I just can't use anything else anymore without feeling frustrated. Theo of T3 Code has made a recent video about its features. A few examples of why I like it: - Not having to use multiple agents (you can switch them mid-conversation with automatic handoff if you want) - The way it handles environments (I can start a new session on any environment (machine) with two clicks (new thread -> pick project on any environment) - I can ask for visual responses (uses a T3 Code tool and renders a html page inside chat with cards, charts, etc. that follow the currently selected color theme (even if you change the theme after the response has been generated) - MCP tools like browser, webfetch, etc. so I don't have to set them up for every agent - Thread handling: Snooze, Settle, Archive, Delete. It's the only tool where I don't get overwhelmed when working on multiple Threads/Projects at the same time (I am diagnosed with ADHD). - Provider usage overview for all registered providers, showing pacing as well - Great citation: when you make a selection in chat, a pill appears and you can create quotation elements that get added to that, can easily be edited or removed (the original reason why I even tried T3 Code in the first place, because it makes responding to long responses incredibly joyful instead of disorienting). I like it so much that I added the same mechanism to my own personal assistant/agent that I host on my VPS. - Great diffing view where you can pick worktree diffs, or any diff from a specific turn in the current thread - Has it's own subagent orchestration that's very pleasant to use - Many more little things that remove a lot of friction and just feel right for me. It's just baffling to me how it is better in every regard than every other harness that I've ever tried (Claude Desktop, Github Copilot App, OpenCode Desktop, all the CLIs, Integrated Agents in VSCode and Zed, etc.) I will still start up a pi on the cli if I just have a quick question because T3 Code needs a bit to start up and connect to all providers/environments. This is my only point of friction: It's a bit heavy on resources (because it does a lot, not because it's slow. I just happen to use it on very old hardware and on one device that is very slowed down due to heavy-handed security scanning). But other than that, I can't imagine using anything else right now. I don't know if I've ever been this exciting about a piece of software. I was very sceptical at first, but quickly fell in love with it.

comments.author: sillysaurusx
comments.text: For example, say you want to search for bugs in 100 code files. Ask Claude to “use subagents to look for bugs across these files” and it will likely spin up 5 agents, each taking a different section of the codebase. Theoretically in the limit case this is 5x faster than Claude doing it without subagents. Any kind of problem shaped like map reduce can be accelerated this way: Looking through your banking records, searching through a database, asking Claude to find that one weird file you remember from three years ago but forgot where you saved it, etc. Just know that there’s no quicker way to hit your limits than to use subagents. So use them if it’s paid for by your work or whenever you need the 5x speed boost.

comments.text: I use AI primarily through work, I don't pay for a personal AI sub. I do have some OpenRouter credits but I mostly use them sparingly to try open weight models out for small personal projects. I currently interact primarily with Claude Code, but most of my async workers are on Codex. The orchestration part is custom. I talk to a "chief of staff" Opus instance to ingest various workstreams (Jira tickets, alerts, personal ideas, etc) and turn them into beads. It launches workers to tackle individual beads using Remuda, an agent launcher I wrote at work in 2025 and open sourced earlier this year:  https://github.com/yendo-eng/remuda . I configure profiles in Remuda that launch containerized agents using my preferred harness and model. I update these profiles as the pareto frontier shifts. Currently it's GPT 6 Luna max for most tasks. It monitors the workers and has them go through at least one round of agentic code review. It surfaces PRs for me to read once they've passed agent review. It then either ships them or hands them off to my coworkers for codebases where I'm not allowed to just merge PRs. Around this workflow I had it write a small collection of skills and scripts to grease the wheels and make repetitive actions more reliable. Since Remuda supports several terminal multiplexers, I've swapped out the backend 3 times: tmux -> herdr-tui -> herdr-core. There's experimental support for Rex but I'm waiting for it to mature a bit before I try and daily drive it. It's not nearly as polished as some of the software factory setups and fancy GUI orchestrators I'm seeing, but it's light, hackable, and so far the bitter lesson has kept this working really well for me so I haven't felt much of a need to try anything else. I have been trying out Muse for a while but it hasn't found a solid place in my life yet. Still too unreliable and too many privacy concerns to justify giving it a lot of access.

comments.text: I'm juggling multiple claude ultra subs, multiple codex $500 a month subs, antigravity for argon, plus API rate deepseek 4.1 flash, mercury 3, and abliterated large v2 for red teaming. I work across multiple models and harnesses using a really simple redis-backed message bus called "nova-bus":  https://github.com/mas-bandwidth/nova-tools  (open source). With just this message bus, I can coordinate AIs to work together at a normal pace (worktrees, subtasks etc...), but past a certain point the AIs can't keep up and I need to use a sprint card system I developed to coordinate work. With this sprint system I'm able to work 200 cards wide (each card is around 30-60 minutes of LLM work in a session) across a fleet of 20 machines linked together with tailscale and ssh. Full system is here:  https://github.com/mas-bandwidth/nova-sprint  (open source) It's been very effective at getting high throughput, but afterwards I find that the resulting code can be a bit of a pastiche from different models working in isolation, thus a good pass over working directly with models to clean up and harden the code is necessary. I find that using nova-bus to coordinate multiple model/harness review of codebase in very effective at increasing code quality. Each model sees things the others don't.

comments.text: I have had a $20 codex subscription. I initially just used codex cloud but more recently have been using opencode with the open chamber ui over the top of it. Codex usage limits have really gone down hill so I also now have a $10 opencode go subscription on which I pretty much just use DeepSeek 4.1 flash. I’ve found DS to be a great model - probably somewhere just below GPT 6.1 Sol but at a fraction of the price. In terms of workflow, I discuss features with chat gpt (because it’s free and it has access to my project’s repo, read only view of prod logs etc, so can make informed decisions). Once we’ve agreed on how a feature should look I ask it to create a spike github issue. I then get another agent in opencode (usually DeepSeek flash or Luna) to break it up into implementation tickets. When I’m ready to build the feature I can give open chamber a list of tickets to work through using the task plugin, so each ticket gets a fresh context. I try to build directly on the main branch and try to ensure we can always deploy to prod even if a feature is half finished (using feature flags etc to switch it off until it’s ready). Once a feature has been implemented I get GPT Sol 6.1 to do exploratory / regression testing with a real browser against a test environment. This usually teases out a lot of edge cases I hadn’t considered and also gives me a chance to improve usability etc. It often takes a few iterations of this (exploratory testing, fixing issues that are found, exploratory testing again…) before a feature is ready to release. I can’t believe how far things have come since August 2025 when I first tried out codex.

comments.author: tritondev
comments.text: I built a Qt GUI-based harness, Humbug, that runs on MacOS, Linux, and Windows (I have reasons to use all 3).  Has only 3 runtime dependencies other than the Python standard library:  https://github.com/m6r-ai/humbug  Usually have 3 or 4 instances running at a time and lets me use LLMs from 9 different providers (and not using their libraries either).  The low dependency approach was slightly limiting early on but now makes it very easy to extend and makes it very easy for an LLM to integrate new features or optimize existing ones. I typically use Claude Sonnet for document-related tasks, and currently DeepSeek 4.1 Flash is my current go to for coding (it's insanely cheap on ollama.com) and I find it's still fast and reliable at very large context lengths.  Previously I used GLM 5.2 a lot and before that was Sonnet for most things. Humbug lets one AI delegate tasks to another and it can choose different models/providers when it does, so works nicely for getting second opinions on things.  I haven't yet found a need for an agent swarm though - more often the parallelism comes from working on multiple projects at the same time. One of the biggest unlocks for me in the last few months is having AIs write ADRs to capture design thinking as a project progresses.  It lets new AI sessions discover the intent behind the current work and surface any potential conflicts that might arise with new requests. One fun feature is the AI can control pretty-much any UI surface the user can control too, and it's quite fun to watch it edit files (you can watch it scrolling around the file in an editor) or use a terminal.  It's a nice visual way to see what's going on.

At work we have both Anthropic and Copilot subscriptions, plus Google AI as it’s included in our business plan anyway.
I have personally been using the Claude Code Desktop App and was happy with it until they made it harder to pick a branch for each worktree! Which is why I tried JetBrains experimental agent IDE, ThinkRail, and I love it! Super easy to start worktrees from any branch and the spec driven development experience they promote is great! It also let me connect to Requesty for my hobby projects and with that I can easily try any model, from any provider. That gave me a much better appreciation of how models perform, how fast and how costly, thanks to Requesty’s super awesome dashboard which is a pleasure to use. I was only using Opus 5.5 before as I wanted the highest quality, but using smaller models you can get much faster work, and the difference in price is dramatic. I have now settled on Haiku 5 for simpler things, it’s nearly free while being really smart still, and for big things I use Opus 5.5 still but also Google Argon 4, it’s incredible as well and it seems to write more human text than Opus. We also have a framework that lets us launch Claude (we could use any harness but for now only Claude) in our Kubernetes cluster within a devcontainer. That lets us ship heavy work off to another machine so our laptop is not overloaded with agents. It works great but we are not open sourcing this framework yet so I cannot link for now. There are some alternatives out there but most of them are out to make big bucks instead of providing a small but powerful solution for this problem.

comments.author: mnahkies
comments.text: I'm using a cli I wrote to orchestrate per-project VMs for sandboxing using libvirt with COW shared golden images to minimise the disk overhead. The VMs get "rebased" periodically onto new golden images for the rootfs, but keep a persistent home FS for longer. I'm going to clean-up the documentation and open source it at some point soon. I was using oh-my-pi, but currently playing around with Hermes as an alternative. Exclusively using open router at the moment, mostly on principle around ZDR, and freedom to experiment with harnesses - but financially I'll probably have to compromise on this soon. GLM, Kimi and DeepSeek are the main models I'm using, with some OpenAI usage. Tmux for remote access and session durability. I'd prefer to find a setup where I could access the same session through a web interface and seamlessly switch back to TUI, ideally spawning sessions through a web hook or similar. I'm going to take a look at Hedr to see if this can improve this. Probably the two major things I'm planning to do next are looking at adding a bifrost VM that will hold all API keys, and centralise management of MCP configuration, potentially use it's skill repo stuff as well. I also want to start controlling egress more - probably iron proxy, though tbh I'd like a solution that was relatively liberal whilst still mitigating exfiltration and prompt injection risks. Maybe I can find a curated allow list to use as a base. Finally, I make a lot of use of open-webui, but it's disjoint from the agentic setup currently - it'd be nice to find a better way to share information/research from it into the agentic sessions.

comments.author: jedisct1
comments.text:
Locally (MBP 128Gb) I have MLX-Serve constantly running with Clef (for model routing and decisions), Qwen-35B-A3B and Ornith-1.5-35B. And I switch to Qwen3.8-27B (the Perplexity Pro version that works well with MLX-Serve) or GLM-5.3-Flash (sushi) when I need to do serious work offline. As a general harness for coding, etc. I use Swival.dev . Configured to use Clef for model routing, with Qwen-35B-A3B for documentation tasks, Ornith to ask questions about code, and various GPT models from a ChatGPT subscription for more difficult tasks. For music, pictures, etc. MLX-Serve is all I use, with the recommended models.
It's really nice. And as a general agent for research, etc. I absolutely love Perplexity. This is by far the AI produce I use the most, ever since it's been available. It's a little bit sad that they are forcing people to use Perplexity Computer, because it's so expensive. But it works incredibly well. Perplexity can now run locally, but even though they include the best Qwen3.8 quant in my experience, the Perplexity tool itself has major issues with context management and tool calling. So, when that doesn't work, I fall back to MLX-Serve and Swival with the Chrome MCP server. For agentic web browsing, I can't live without Comet anymore. So many websites are painful to use, and finding the right buttons to click even to perform very common tasks is a challenge. So, I frequently just ask Comet to do it for me. I also use it to compare products, compare places on AirBNB, write personalized messages on Instagram, etc. As for an OpenClaw-like tool, I'm using NBClaw. I was initially very excited about it. Look, I can just send messages on Signal and let the agent do work for me! And I occasionally found it useful to remotely fix issues on the host it was running on, or long tasks such as making sure that all my projects worked with a new version of the Zig compiler. It became a replacement for Perplexity because, hey, it's cool, everything's running locally, using my own web browser, etc. But eventually, I used it less and less. Nowadays, I still enjoy the fact that it's sending me a summary of cool things it found in Hacker News and research papers on topics I'm interesting in. But that's pretty much it. I don't use it much for agentic tasks anymore. It still happens (I recently used it to fix a bug in an opensource project while I was on the bus), but mostly just only when I ran out of Perplexity Computer credits.
